source: Share of firms using AI in 2026: around one in four (GO-Science AI Scenarios 2030 p54, citing DSIT/ONS 2026). The model measures AI change relative to this level

Cut in youth job openings (vacancies) in a fully exposed occupation at today's level of AI use, compared with no AI. Hires fall by less (roughly alpha times this). Informed by Stanford's 19% employment gap for 22-25 year olds (Brynjolfsson et al. 2026) and KCL's 23.4% fall in postings for highly exposed roles (Klein Teeselink 2025, all ages). Range 10-30%. Scales in a straight line with the share of firms using AI. RG judgement

How strongly hires respond to the number of job openings (the elasticity in a standard Cobb-Douglas matching function). The range 0.3-0.7 is RG judgement around the commonly used value of 0.5. It is the single most important assumption for the size of the post-2030 effects

How much job losses among existing workers respond compared with the cut in hiring. Below 1 because current evidence shows firms adjust through hiring rather than letting people go (Stanford Canaries Aug 2026; GO-Science p56)

Share of inactive young people who go back into education each quarter. RG assumption
Share of employed young people who go back into education each quarter. RG assumption

Young people Milburn's package moves into work by 2036/37, thousands (analytical annex s.4 and s.8; report para 111)

Share of the into-work effect that comes from hiring subsidies (the rest comes from job support). Central value is the cost share 1.1/(1.1+1.9+0.7) from Milburn's costings (annex Table 1), because Milburn does not publish NEET effects by policy. RG assumption
AI-proofing test: a policy passes if it keeps at least this share of its no-AI effect in every scenario, judged at the median run and at the 10th percentile run
Monte Carlo runs per scenario

Average length, in quarters, of a Milburn-funded education or training place (4 = one year; sensitivity 8). When it ends, the learner looks for work like any other education leaver. RG assumption
